claim: Mtb infection induced a quiescent energy phenotype in human monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Mtb infection induced a quiescent energy phenotype in human monocyte-derived macrophages and decelerated flux through glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from extracellular flux analysis showing shifts in bioenergetic phenotypes (Figure 4) and 13C-tracing experiments (Figure 6).

claim: Mtb infection decelerated flux through glycolysis and the TCA cycle in human monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Mtb infection induced a quiescent energy phenotype in human monocyte-derived macrophages and decelerated flux through glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
evidence: Supported by 13C-tracing data showing reduced enrichment in glycolytic and TCA metabolites (Figure 6).

claim: Infection with M. bovis BCG induced glycolytic phenotypes with greater flux compared to Mtb infection.
source: In contrast, infection with the vaccine strain, M. bovis BCG, or dead Mtb induced glycolytic phenotypes with greater flux.
evidence: Supported by extracellular flux analysis data showing increased glycolytic parameters in BCG-infected cells (Figures 3, 5).

claim: Dead Mtb infection induced glycolytic phenotypes with greater flux compared to live Mtb infection.
source: In contrast, infection with the vaccine strain, M. bovis BCG, or dead Mtb induced glycolytic phenotypes with greater flux.
evidence: Supported by extracellular flux analysis data showing increased glycolytic parameters in dead Mtb-infected cells compared to live Mtb (Figures 3, 5).

claim: Mtb reduced the mitochondrial dependency on glucose in infected macrophages.
source: Furthermore, Mtb reduced the mitochondrial dependency on glucose and increased the mitochondrial dependency on fatty acids, shifting this dependency from endogenous fatty acids in uninfected cells to exogenous fatty acids in infected macrophages.
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial fuel test data showing decreased glucose dependency in Mtb-infected hMDMs (Figure 7C).

claim: Mtb increased the mitochondrial dependency on fatty acids in infected macrophages.
source: Furthermore, Mtb reduced the mitochondrial dependency on glucose and increased the mitochondrial dependency on fatty acids, shifting this dependency from endogenous fatty acids in uninfected cells to exogenous fatty acids in infected macrophages.
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial fuel test data showing increased fatty acid dependency in Mtb-infected cells (Figure 7).

claim: Mtb shifted mitochondrial dependency from endogenous fatty acids in uninfected cells to exogenous fatty acids in infected macrophages.
source: Furthermore, Mtb reduced the mitochondrial dependency on glucose and increased the mitochondrial dependency on fatty acids, shifting this dependency from endogenous fatty acids in uninfected cells to exogenous fatty acids in infected macrophages.
evidence: Supported by fatty acid oxidation assay data showing differential utilization of endogenous vs. exogenous fatty acids (Figure 7D-L).

claim: Quantifiable bioenergetic parameters of the host can be used to accurately measure and track disease.
source: We demonstrate how quantifiable bioenergetic parameters of the host can be used to accurately measure and track disease, which will enable rapid quantifiable assessment of drug and vaccine efficacy.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive bioenergetic profiling data presented throughout the manuscript showing distinct differences between pathogenic and non-pathogenic infections.

claim: Bioenergetic parameters will enable rapid quantifiable assessment of drug and vaccine efficacy.
source: We demonstrate how quantifiable bioenergetic parameters of the host can be used to accurately measure and track disease, which will enable rapid quantifiable assessment of drug and vaccine efficacy.
evidence: Inferred from the ability to distinguish between pathogenic and non-pathogenic infections using bioenergetic parameters.

claim: Mtb is the etiological agent of tuberculosis (TB).
source: Mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis induced by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiological agent of tuberculosis (TB), are poorly understood, and increasing evidence suggests that Mtb subverts the host's immune response to establish a persistent infection (Cambier et al., 2014; Hmama et al., 2015; Józefowski et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on Mtb pathogenesis.

claim: Mtb subverts the host's immune response to establish a persistent infection.
source: Mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis induced by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiological agent of tuberculosis (TB), are poorly understood, and increasing evidence suggests that Mtb subverts the host's immune response to establish a persistent infection (Cambier et al., 2014; Hmama et al., 2015; Józefowski et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on Mtb immune evasion.

claim: Metabolic plasticity of immune cells is crucial to the success of the immune system to control microbial infection.
source: Crucial to the success of the immune system to control microbial infection is the metabolic plasticity of immune cells to activate antimicrobial mechanisms in macrophages and activate T cells in response to microbial invasion.
evidence: Based on established understanding of immune cell metabolism.

claim: Precise coordination between diverse metabolic pathways underlies metabolic plasticity of immune cells.
source: Precise coordination between diverse metabolic pathways underlies this plasticity (Ganeshan and Chawla, 2014; Loftus and Finlay, 2016; Mathis and Shoelson, 2011), which is disrupted by pathogenic bacteria.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on immune cell metabolism.

claim: Metabolic plasticity of immune cells is disrupted by pathogenic bacteria.
source: Precise coordination between diverse metabolic pathways underlies this plasticity (Ganeshan and Chawla, 2014; Loftus and Finlay, 2016; Mathis and Shoelson, 2011), which is disrupted by pathogenic bacteria.
evidence: Supported by citations and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Host-directed therapies are increasingly considered for adjunctive treatment of tuberculosis.
source: Hence, host-directed therapies are increasingly considered for adjunctive treatment of tuberculosis (Guler and Brombacher, 2015; Mahon and Hafner, 2015; Wallis and Hafner, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on host-directed TB therapies.

claim: Mtb adaptation to the host environment requires catabolism of host-derived lipids.
source: Studies suggest that Mtb pathogenicity is reinforced with participation of metabolic pathways from the host, including evidence suggesting that Mtb adaptation to the host environment requires catabolism of host-derived lipids (Daniel et al., 2011; Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008; Rohde et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on Mtb lipid metabolism.

claim: Mtb regulates metabolic thresholds of the host macrophage.
source: This is assumed to be induced through Mtb regulating metabolic thresholds of the host macrophage (Mehrotra et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: There is a shift from oxidative phosphorylation towards glycolysis in macrophages infected with an avirulent strain (H37Ra) or dead γ-irradiated Mtb.
source: Recent studies suggested that there is a shift from oxidative phosphorylation towards glycolysis in macrophages infected with an avirulent strain (H37Ra) or dead γ-irradiated Mtb (Gleeson et al., 2016), and in Mtb (H37Rv)-infected mouse lungs using transcriptomic profiling and confocal imaging (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: There is a shift from oxidative phosphorylation towards glycolysis in Mtb (H37Rv)-infected mouse lungs.
source: Recent studies suggested that there is a shift from oxidative phosphorylation towards glycolysis in macrophages infected with an avirulent strain (H37Ra) or dead γ-irradiated Mtb (Gleeson et al., 2016), and in Mtb (H37Rv)-infected mouse lungs using transcriptomic profiling and confocal imaging (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: The switch to aerobic glycolysis observed in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells stimulated with dead Mtb lysate is TLR2-dependent.
source: Lachmandas et al. (Lachmandas et al., 2016) demonstrated that the switch to aerobic glycolysis observed in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells stimulated with dead Mtb lysate is TLR2-dependent, and is mediated in part through the AKT-mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: The switch to aerobic glycolysis in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells stimulated with dead Mtb lysate is mediated in part through the AKT-mTOR pathway.
source: Lachmandas et al. (Lachmandas et al., 2016) demonstrated that the switch to aerobic glycolysis observed in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells stimulated with dead Mtb lysate is TLR2-dependent, and is mediated in part through the AKT-mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: The actual underlying mechanisms with live virulent Mtb infection enabling it to persist in humans remain elusive.
source: While this evidence supports the conclusion that dead Mtb reprograms host energy metabolism, the actual underlying mechanisms with live virulent Mtb infection enabling it to persist in humans remain elusive.
evidence: Based on the gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: The metabolic health of the Mtb-infected cell is poorly defined.
source: Furthermore, the metabolic health of the Mtb-infected cell is poorly defined as there is a lack of knowledge on exactly what metabolic health comprises, and what should be measured.
evidence: Based on the gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: Aberrant cellular bioenergetics have been associated with diseases such as diabetes, cancer, neurodegeneration, and cardiac disease.
source: Aberrant cellular bioenergetics have been associated with, and are often the cause of, diseases such as diabetes, cancer, neurodegeneration, and cardiac disease.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Dysfunctional energy metabolism in diseases has been successfully investigated using extracellular flux (XF) analysis.
source: The dysfunctional energy metabolism in these diseases has been successfully investigated using extracellular flux (XF) analysis (Devarajan et al., 2011; Hill et al., 2009; Salabei et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2017; Cronin-Furman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research using XF analysis.

claim: XF analysis monitors the rate of oxygen consumed by cells (oxygen consumption rate, OCR) and the release of protons from the cells into the extracellular medium (extracellular acidification rate, ECAR) non-invasively in real time.
source: XF analysis monitors the rate of oxygen consumed by cells (oxygen consumption rate, OCR) and the release of protons from the cells into the extracellular medium (extracellular acidification rate, ECAR) non-invasively in real time (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the technical capabilities of the XF analysis platform, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Cells use two main pathways to produce ATP, namely oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolysis.
source: Measurements of cellular respiration and acidification form the foundation of our understanding of bioenergetics because cells use two main pathways to produce ATP, namely oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolysis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism.

claim: XF analysis technology is largely unexplored in the field of bacterial pathogenesis.
source: This technology is largely unexplored in the field of bacterial pathogenesis, with a few studies focused on Helicobacter pylori infections (Hammond et al., 2015; Saha et al., 2010), but studies on live virulent Mtb pathogenesis are lacking.
evidence: Based on literature review showing limited application to bacterial pathogenesis.

claim: Studies on live virulent Mtb pathogenesis using XF analysis are lacking.
source: This technology is largely unexplored in the field of bacterial pathogenesis, with a few studies focused on Helicobacter pylori infections (Hammond et al., 2015; Saha et al., 2010), but studies on live virulent Mtb pathogenesis are lacking.
evidence: Based on literature review showing gap in knowledge.

claim: 106 Mtb consumed 10–20 pmoles O2/min.
source: Firstly, we have previously demonstrated that 106 Mtb consumed 10–20 pmoles O2/min (Lamprecht et al., 2016) in contrast to 100–200 pmoles O2/min consumed by 80 000 to 100 000 macrophages under the basal conditions measured in this study.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: 80,000 to 100,000 macrophages consumed 100–200 pmoles O2/min under basal conditions.
source: Firstly, we have previously demonstrated that 106 Mtb consumed 10–20 pmoles O2/min (Lamprecht et al., 2016) in contrast to 100–200 pmoles O2/min consumed by 80 000 to 100 000 macrophages under the basal conditions measured in this study.
evidence: Based on measurements in the current study.

claim: At a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1, 105 Mtb would result in a negligible contribution (<1 pmoles O2/min) to the OCR of the uninfected macrophages.
source: Thus, at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1, 105 Mtb would result in a negligible contribution (<1 pmoles O2/min) to the OCR of the uninfected macrophages.
evidence: Based on calculation from the OCR values of Mtb and macrophages.

claim: Mtb infection at MOI of 1 and 2.5 progressively decreases the basal respiration (OCR) of both THP-1 macrophages and hMDMs relative to that of uninfected macrophages.
source: Thirdly, Mtb infection at MOI of 1 and 2.5 progressively decreases the basal respiration (OCR) of both THP-1 macrophages and hMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) relative to that of uninfected macrophages.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Less than 200 CFU were obtained per well from the washes of the infected hMDMs (MOI 5).
source: When the washes of the macrophages were plated out on 7H11 agar plates, less than 200 CFU were obtained per well from the washes of the infected hMDMs (MOI 5), and less than 100 CFU per well from the infected THP-1 cells (MOI 5).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements of CFU from washes.

claim: Less than 100 CFU per well were obtained from the infected THP-1 cells (MOI 5).
source: When the washes of the macrophages were plated out on 7H11 agar plates, less than 200 CFU were obtained per well from the washes of the infected hMDMs (MOI 5), and less than 100 CFU per well from the infected THP-1 cells (MOI 5).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements of CFU from washes.

claim: The OCR and ECAR readings obtained from extracellular bacteria in the final wash were below 0 pmol/min and at 0 mpH/min, respectively.
source: The OCR and ECAR readings obtained were below 0 pmol/min and at 0 mpH/min, respectively, and the extracellular bacteria did not respond to the sequential injections of oligomycin, FCCP and rotenone and antimycin A (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: The infecting mycobacteria do not contribute to the measured OCR of the infected macrophages under the experimental conditions.
source: Thus, the infecting mycobacteria do not contribute to the measured OCR of the infected macrophages under our conditions.
evidence: Based on multiple lines of evidence including OCR measurements of extracellular bacteria and calculations.

claim: There was an increase in the percentage of infected cells with an increase in MOI of both the THP-1 cells and the hMDMs.
source: We found that there was an increase in the percentage of infected cells with an increase in MOI of both the THP-1 cells and the hMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–G.

claim: Lipids shed by intracellular mycobacteria, such as TDM and PIM2, spread via the endocytic network throughout the macrophage, and via exocytic vesicles to neighboring uninfected cells.
source: Although the percentage of uninfected cells will contribute to the readout of the XF profiles, previous studies have demonstrated that lipids shed by intracellular mycobacteria, such as TDM and PIM2, spread via the endocytic network throughout the macrophage, and via exocytic vesicles to neighboring uninfected cells (Beatty et al., 2000; Xu et al., 1994) and can elicit the production of proinflammatory cytokines (Rhoades et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Lipids shed by intracellular mycobacteria can elicit the production of proinflammatory cytokines.
source: Although the percentage of uninfected cells will contribute to the readout of the XF profiles, previous studies have demonstrated that lipids shed by intracellular mycobacteria, such as TDM and PIM2, spread via the endocytic network throughout the macrophage, and via exocytic vesicles to neighboring uninfected cells (Beatty et al., 2000; Xu et al., 1994) and can elicit the production of proinflammatory cytokines (Rhoades et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: The bioenergetic metabolism of the 'by-stander' uninfected cells will also be modulated by lipids shed from infected cells.
source: Consequently, the bioenergetic metabolism of the 'by-stander' uninfected cells will also be modulated.
evidence: Inferred from the evidence that shed lipids spread to uninfected cells and elicit responses.

claim: Infection of THP-1 macrophages with Mtb or BCG significantly decreased basal respiration, ATP-linked OCR, proton leak and maximal respiration.
source: Figure 2A and B shows that infection of THP-1 macrophages with Mtb or BCG significantly decreased the respiratory parameters: Basal Resp, ATP-linked OCR, proton leak and Max Resp (and SRC in the case of Mtb), and increased Non-Mito Resp.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Mtb infection of THP-1 macrophages significantly decreased spare respiratory capacity (SRC).
source: Figure 2A and B shows that infection of THP-1 macrophages with Mtb or BCG significantly decreased the respiratory parameters: Basal Resp, ATP-linked OCR, proton leak and Max Resp (and SRC in the case of Mtb), and increased Non-Mito Resp.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Mtb and BCG infection of THP-1 macrophages increased non-mitochondrial respiration.
source: Figure 2A and B shows that infection of THP-1 macrophages with Mtb or BCG significantly decreased the respiratory parameters: Basal Resp, ATP-linked OCR, proton leak and Max Resp (and SRC in the case of Mtb), and increased Non-Mito Resp.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Infection with dead Mtb only significantly reduced the respiratory parameters at MOIs of 2.5 and 5.
source: Infection with the dead Mtb only significantly reduced the respiratory parameters at MOIs of 2.5 and 5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D and Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D and Figure 2A–B.

claim: Mtb infection of hMDMs dramatically reduced the respiratory parameters of the macrophage.
source: Mtb infection of hMDMs dramatically reduced the respiratory parameters of the macrophage, while significantly increasing Non-Mito Resp (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: Mtb infection of hMDMs significantly increased non-mitochondrial respiration.
source: Mtb infection of hMDMs dramatically reduced the respiratory parameters of the macrophage, while significantly increasing Non-Mito Resp (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: BCG infection increased the maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity of the hMDMs at all MOIs investigated.
source: Notably, contrary to Mtb, BCG infection increased the Max Resp and SRC of the hMDMs at all MOIs investigated.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: At a MOI of 5, BCG decreased the basal respiration, ATP-linked OCR and proton leak of hMDMs, while increasing the non-mitochondrial respiration.
source: At a MOI of 5, BCG decreased the Basal Resp, ATP-linked OCR and proton leak, while increasing the Non-Mito Resp (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: Dead Mtb did not affect the respiratory parameters of the hMDMs at MOIs of 1 and 5.
source: Dead Mtb did not affect the respiratory parameters of the hMDMs at MOIs of 1 and 5, but a MOI of 2.5 increased the Max Resp and SRC of the macrophages as in the BCG infection (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Dead Mtb at a MOI of 2.5 increased the maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity of hMDMs.
source: Dead Mtb did not affect the respiratory parameters of the hMDMs at MOIs of 1 and 5, but a MOI of 2.5 increased the Max Resp and SRC of the macrophages as in the BCG infection (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Spare respiratory capacity (SRC) reflects the ability of the cell to increase respiration to increase the supply of ATP in scenarios when the energy demand exceeds supply under conditions of stress or increased work load.
source: SRC is an important parameter that reflects the ability of the cell to increase respiration to increase the supply of ATP in scenarios when the energy demand exceeds supply under conditions of stress or increased work load.
evidence: Based on established understanding of cellular bioenergetics.

claim: An increase in the SRC of hMDMs following infection with potential vaccine candidates may aid identification of promising candidates.
source: Thus, an increase in the SRC of hMDMs following infection with potential vaccine candidates may aid identification of promising candidates.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BCG increases SRC while Mtb decreases it.

claim: Pharmacological killing of Mtb will not fully restore the macrophage's bioenergetic metabolism to that of the uninfected macrophage.
source: This has implications for pharmacological killing of Mtb, as killing intracellular Mtb will not fully restore the macrophage's bioenergetic metabolism to that of the uninfected macrophage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dead Mtb infection still alters bioenergetic metabolism.

claim: Pharmacological killing will improve the bioenergetic profile of the live Mtb-infected macrophages, in particular, the ATP-linked respiration and the non-mitochondrial respiration.
source: However, pharmacological killing will improve the bioenergetic profile of the live Mtb-infected macrophages, in particular, the ATP-linked Resp and the Non-Mito Resp.
evidence: Inferred from comparing the bioenergetic profiles of live Mtb vs. dead Mtb infections.

claim: Improvements in ATP-linked respiration and non-mitochondrial respiration can be used as indicators of effective pharmacological killing of Mtb during screening of potential anti-TB drug leads in Mtb-infected macrophages.
source: Therefore, improvements in these parameters of the infected macrophages can be used as indicators of effective pharmacological killing of Mtb during screening of potential anti-TB drug leads in Mtb-infected macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the bioenergetic differences between live and dead Mtb infections.

claim: All the mycobacterial strains reduced the glycolytic parameters of THP-1 cells at MOIs of 5.
source: In THP-1 cells, all the mycobacterial strains reduced the glycolytic parameters at MOIs of 5 (Figure 3A–B) and 2.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), with dead Mtb having the least effects.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: All the mycobacterial strains reduced the glycolytic parameters of THP-1 cells at MOIs of 2.5, with dead Mtb having the least effects.
source: In THP-1 cells, all the mycobacterial strains reduced the glycolytic parameters at MOIs of 5 (Figure 3A–B) and 2.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), with dead Mtb having the least effects.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: At a MOI of 1, Mtb decreased the glycolytic parameters of THP-1 cells.
source: At a MOI of 1, Mtb decreased the glycolytic parameters, BCG increased the glycolytic parameters and dead Mtb had no effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: At a MOI of 1, BCG increased the glycolytic parameters of THP-1 cells.
source: At a MOI of 1, Mtb decreased the glycolytic parameters, BCG increased the glycolytic parameters and dead Mtb had no effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: At a MOI of 1, dead Mtb had no effect on the glycolytic parameters of THP-1 cells.
source: At a MOI of 1, Mtb decreased the glycolytic parameters, BCG increased the glycolytic parameters and dead Mtb had no effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Mtb at a MOI of 2.5 had little effect on the glycolytic parameters of hMDMs.
source: In hMDMs, Mtb at a MOI of 2.5 had little effect and at a MOI of 1 increased glucose metabolism extracellular acidification. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Mtb at a MOI of 1 increased glucose metabolism extracellular acidification in hMDMs.
source: In hMDMs, Mtb at a MOI of 2.5 had little effect and at a MOI of 1 increased glucose metabolism extracellular acidification. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: BCG and dead Mtb infection of hMDMs increased glucose metabolism acidification and the glycolytic capacity at all MOIs investigated.
source: Contrary to THP-1 cells, BCG and dead Mtb infection of hMDMs increased glucose metabolism acidification and the glycolytic capacity at all MOIs investigated.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Increases in the non-glycolytic acidification were observed in the BCG and dead Mtb infections of hMDMs.
source: Increases in the non-glycolytic acidification were observed in the BCG and dead Mtb infections, probably as a result of the carbonic acid produced from CO2 generated by the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Mtb infection significantly reduced glucose metabolism extracellular acidification in the macrophages.
source: In sum, marked glycolytic differences were observed between the virulent and non-virulent infections, with Mtb infection significantly reducing glucose metabolism extracellular acidification in the macrophages.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mtb infection exhibited the most pronounced shift from an Energetic phenotype towards that of a Quiescent phenotype with increasing MOI in THP-1 cells and hMDMs.
source: In THP-1 cells and hMDMs, infection with Mtb exhibited the most pronounced shift from an Energetic phenotype towards that of a Quiescent phenotype with increasing MOI (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claim: BCG and dead Mtb infections of THP-1 cells (MOIs 2.5 and 5) induced much smaller shifts towards quiescence compared to Mtb.
source: In contrast, BCG and dead Mtb infections of THP-1 cells (MOIs 2.5 and 5) induced much smaller shifts towards quiescence (Figure 4B and C); whereas in hMDMs, only BCG infection at a MOI of 5 engendered a small shift towards quiescence.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: In hMDMs, only BCG infection at a MOI of 5 engendered a small shift towards quiescence.
source: In contrast, BCG and dead Mtb infections of THP-1 cells (MOIs 2.5 and 5) induced much smaller shifts towards quiescence (Figure 4B and C); whereas in hMDMs, only BCG infection at a MOI of 5 engendered a small shift towards quiescence.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dead Mtb did not affect the OCR of the hMDMs but decreased the ECAR at lower MOIs.
source: Dead Mtb did not affect the OCR of the hMDMs but decreased the ECAR at lower MOIs (Figure 4F), again underscoring the differences between live and dead Mtb.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mtb infection shifts the energy phenotypes of human macrophages towards a metabolic quiescent state.
source: In sum, our data clearly demonstrate that Mtb infection shifts the energy phenotypes of human macrophages towards a metabolic quiescent state.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In XF analysis, bulk acidification of the extracellular medium, as measured by ECAR, is not specific for glycolysis as the mitochondrial TCA produces CO2 that is partially hydrated in the extracellular medium and contributes to the acidification of the extracellular medium.
source: In XF analysis, bulk acidification of the extracellular medium, as measured by ECAR, is not specific for glycolysis as the mitochondrial TCA produces CO2 that is partially hydrated in the extracellular medium and contributes to the acidification of the extracellular medium (Mookerjee et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on XF analysis methodology.

claim: Mtb significantly reduces the basal and compensatory glycolytic rates of THP-1 cells (MOI 2.5 and 5).
source: An immediate observation is that Mtb significantly reduces the basal and compensatory glycolytic rates of THP-1 cells (MOI 2.5 and 5, Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: BCG and dead Mtb infections increased the basal glycolytic rates of THP-1 cells at all MOIs examined.
source: In contrast, BCG and dead Mtb infections increased the basal glycolytic rates of THP-1 cells at all MOIs examined.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Compensatory glycolysis was increased in BCG-infected THP-1 cells at all MOIs.
source: Furthermore, compensatory glycolysis was increased in BCG-infected cells at all MOIs, and in dead Mtb infections at a MOI of 1.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Compensatory glycolysis was increased in dead Mtb infections of THP-1 cells at a MOI of 1.
source: Furthermore, compensatory glycolysis was increased in BCG-infected cells at all MOIs, and in dead Mtb infections at a MOI of 1.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Mtb (MOI 5) decreased both the glycolytic rate and the compensatory glycolytic rate significantly in hMDMs.
source: In hMDMs, Mtb (MOI 5) decreased both the glycolytic rate and the compensatory glycolytic rate significantly (Figure 5D–E), but lower MOIs (1 and 2.5) did not affect the glycolytic rates of hMDMs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D–E.

claim: Lower MOIs (1 and 2.5) of Mtb did not affect the glycolytic rates of hMDMs.
source: In hMDMs, Mtb (MOI 5) decreased both the glycolytic rate and the compensatory glycolytic rate significantly (Figure 5D–E), but lower MOIs (1 and 2.5) did not affect the glycolytic rates of hMDMs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L.

claim: BCG infection increased both the glycolytic rate and the compensatory glycolytic rates of hMDMs at all MOIs.
source: BCG infection increased both the glycolytic rate and the compensatory glycolytic rates at all MOIs, whereas dead Mtb had no effect (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L.

claim: Dead Mtb had no effect on the glycolytic rates of hMDMs.
source: BCG infection increased both the glycolytic rate and the compensatory glycolytic rates at all MOIs, whereas dead Mtb had no effect (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L.

claim: Mtb decreases the glycolytic PER in human macrophages at higher mycobacterial burdens.
source: In sum, profound differences were observed in the glycoPER of infections with virulent versus non-virulent mycobacterial strains. Noticeably, Mtb decreases the glycolytic PER in human macrophages at higher mycobacterial burdens, whereas BCG increases the glycolytic PER.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: BCG increases the glycolytic PER in human macrophages.
source: In sum, profound differences were observed in the glycoPER of infections with virulent versus non-virulent mycobacterial strains. Noticeably, Mtb decreases the glycolytic PER in human macrophages at higher mycobacterial burdens, whereas BCG increases the glycolytic PER.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dead Mtb infection increases the glycoPER in THP-1 cells.
source: However, dead Mtb infection increases the glycoPER in THP-1 cells and has no effect in hMDMs.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dead Mtb infection has no effect on glycoPER in hMDMs.
source: However, dead Mtb infection increases the glycoPER in THP-1 cells and has no effect in hMDMs.
